How we know
The story

The Trevi Fountain, finished in 1762, shows Oceanus, god of the sea, riding a shell chariot pulled by sea horses, one wild and one calm, for the moods of the sea. The water comes from an aqueduct built in 19 BC. Tradition says that if you throw a coin over your left shoulder with your right hand, you'll return to Rome. About €3,000 is collected each day and given to charity.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR
The wild and calm sea horses.
Oceanus at the center.

Privacy

Draft, lawyer review before launch. Not yet reviewed by a lawyer; it will be before Kairoute is sold or published in an app store.

Effective November 10, 2026

Kairoute is built to keep your trip yours. This policy explains what the app stores, what it sends, and the choices you have.

What stays on your device
Your trips, itineraries, hotels, cruise details and preferences.
City guides the app has built for you.
Your journal: notes, ratings and photos.

The preview has no accounts. We do not see this information unless you share it.

What is sent to provide the AI guide

When you build a guide, import an itinerary, ask the guide a question or translate a story, the text or photo you provide is sent to our AI provider to produce the answer. Do not include passport numbers, payment details or other sensitive information in itinerary photos.

Location

Kairoute uses your device's location only if you allow it: to show where you are on the day's map, to notice when you reach a stop on the tour, and to time the back-to-the-ship countdown from where you are. To work out the walk or ride from there, that starting point is sent to Kairoute's helper. If you lead a group trip, a regroup call shares your location with the group. You can turn location off at any time in your device's settings.

What we do not do
We do not sell your personal information.
We do not show third-party ads or use advertising trackers.
We do not build a profile of you for marketing.
Sharing a trip

When you share or export a trip, the people you send it to can see everything in it. Shared copies are under their control.

Deleting your data

Delete a single trip from the home screen, or clear everything in Settings, Start over. Uninstalling the app or clearing your browser data also removes it.

Children

Kairoute is not directed to children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect their information.

Changes and contact

If this policy changes, we will update the date above and tell you in the app. Questions: wovenleafapps@gmail.com.

Effective November 20, 2026

By using Kairoute you agree to these terms. If you do not agree, please do not use the app.

A planning guide with estimated times

Kairoute suggests routes, times, places to eat and stories about the sights. Opening hours, prices, port times, transit and closures change. Always confirm important details with the venue, your cruise line, airline or rail operator.

Getting back on time is your responsibility

Leave-by times, back-by times and countdowns are estimates. Kairoute pads them with spare time (on a port day it plans you back at least 45 minutes before all aboard), but traffic, queues, weather, strikes and changes to timetables can still make a trip take longer.

The official time is always the one your cruise line, airline or rail operator gives you: the ship's all-aboard time, your boarding time or your departure. Kairoute shows the ship's all-aboard time next to its own times so you can check them against each other. Confirm it on the day, as it can change.

You are responsible for being back aboard your ship, at your gate or on your train on time. Kairoute is not liable for missed ships, flights, trains, connections, tours or bookings, or for any costs that follow from them.

AI content

1
Trevi Fountain

Fountain · 20 min · Must-see

Local name: Fontana di Trevi

Rome's most famous baroque fountain.

WHAT'S HERE, IN WALKING ORDER
Arriving 9:15 am
Stand here: Come into the little square and find a spot with a clear view of the fountain.
And suddenly, there it is: the Trevi Fountain, tucked into this small square among the side streets. It's the largest Baroque fountain in the world, 86 feet high and about 161 feet wide, finished in 1762. Crowds gather here, and so do pickpockets. Keep your bag zipped and in front of you. To go down to the water's edge and throw a coin, visitors now usually need a 2-euro ticket during the day; late at night the barriers open. Check on the day. The name comes from the Latin trivium, the meeting of three streets.
▶ Play
Reading the fountain 9:19 am
Stand here: Stay facing the center of the fountain.
The theme is the taming of the waters. In the central niche stands Oceanus, by the sculptor Pietro Bracci, on a shell chariot, with tritons wrestling sea horses below him. On either side of him are two figures. One is Abundance, pouring water from her urn. The other is Salubrity, health, holding a cup that a snake drinks from. This water has a long history. The fountain is the end of an aqueduct that goes back to 19 BC, the Aqua Virgo, and it is still in use today. Look up at the carved panels above: they show how the aqueduct began. Legend has it that a virgin helped Roman engineers find the spring.
▶ Play
How it was built 9:23 am
Stand here: Step a little to one side so you can see the whole width of the palace behind the fountain.
The fountain is built right onto the back of a palace, the Palazzo Poli. It took more than a century of tries to get it built. In 1629 Pope Urban VIII asked Bernini for ideas, but the pope died and the plan was dropped. Then in 1730 there was a contest. Nicola Salvi lost, to a man from Florence, and Romans were so outraged that Salvi got the job anyway. Work began in 1732. Salvi died in 1751 with the fountain half done, and Giuseppe Pannini finished it. Most of it is travertine, a pale stone quarried near Tivoli, about 22 miles east of Rome. Pannini changed the plan at the end: instead of statues of Agrippa and of Trivia, the Roman virgin, he put in the figures you see now. Pope Clement XIII opened it on May 22, 1762. A barber's ugly shop sign would have spoiled the effect, so Salvi hid it behind a big sculpted vase. Romans call it the Ace of Cups.
▶ Play
The coin 9:27 am
Stand here: Turn so your back is to the fountain.
Now the tradition. Throw a coin into the fountain before you leave Rome, and it's believed you'll come back. You throw it with your back to the water, right hand over your left shoulder. By one estimate, some 3,000 euros go in every day, and the money is given to the charity Caritas. So your wish helps someone else. Some people try to fish the coins out. It's illegal, and it happens regularly anyway. The night lighting owes something to the fashion house Fendi, which paid for a 20-month restoration, the most thorough in the fountain's history. It was finished in November 2015 and added more than 100 LED lights. And it has its own music. Respighi's 1916 piece Fountains of Rome includes a movement called The Trevi Fountain at Noon. The fountain is a film star too: in Roman Holiday, in Three Coins in the Fountain, and in La Dolce Vita, where Anita Ekberg wades in with Marcello Mastroianni.
▶ Play
Closing 9:31 am
Stand here: Take one last look before you go.
Everyone here is hoping for the same small thing: to come back. Whether or not the coin works, it's a good wish to make.
